49900: How to read the whole Bible with Jesus as the key: progressive revelation, how Jesus and Paul read the Scriptures, and how the Word made flesh interprets the hard texts, the types and shadows, and the prophecies. Each lesson gives the Jesus-lens reading its full voice and sets the other serious readings beside it.
49901: Hard Texts: Violence, Accommodation and Changing Perception
49902: The Bible says God ordered a massacre and then says God will punish it. He says something and we understand something. How do we read the violent parts of the Old Testament if Jesus shows us what God is like?
49903: Every Christian reads the violent texts through some lens; the real questions are which lens, and how honestly we use it. One serious view says the Old Testament records a real but developing human perception of God that is corrected in Christ; other serious views say God truly commanded these things in a unique, limited setting, or that the canon deliberately leaves the tension open. Know all of them, and know that misused texts have cost real lives.
49905:
The Old Testament contains passages where God is said to command or approve terrible violence. In Deuteronomy Israel is told to "utterly destroy" the nations of Canaan and to show them no mercy. In 1 Samuel 15 Saul is told to kill the Amalekites, "both man and woman, infant and suckling". A psalm blesses whoever dashes Babylon's babies against the rock. These are not obscure footnotes; they are in the text, and serious readers of every kind find them painful.

The learner put it this way: "He says something and we understand something." In other words, there is God's speaking, and there is how fallen people heard, understood and wrote it down. Whether that gap exists, how big it is, and how we can tell, is the real question of this lesson.

Jesus himself raises the issue. Asked about divorce, he says Moses allowed it "because of the hardness of your hearts: but from the beginning it was not so" (Matthew 19:8). So at least one law in the Torah was, by Jesus' own account, a concession to human hardness rather than a full picture of God's will. Every view in this lesson has to account for that verse.
49907:
In 2 Kings 9–10 a prophet sent by Elisha anoints the army commander Jehu as king of Israel and tells him to strike down the house of Ahab, as judgement for the blood of the prophets and of Naboth. Jehu kills King Joram at Jezreel, has Jezebel thrown from a window, has seventy sons of Ahab beheaded, kills Ahab's officials, friends and priests, kills forty-two relatives of King Ahaziah of Judah, and then traps and slaughters the worshippers of Baal in their temple. Afterwards the narrator reports God saying: "Because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes... thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel" (2 Kings 10:30). The very next verse adds that Jehu did not walk in God's law with all his heart and kept Jeroboam's golden calves.

About a century later, Hosea is told to name his son Jezreel, "for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu" (Hosea 1:4). The Hebrew verb is *paqad*, literally "visit": God will visit the bloodshed of Jezreel on Jehu's dynasty. Jehu's last descendant, Zechariah, was assassinated after six months on the throne (2 Kings 15:8-12), fulfilling both the promise of four generations and Hosea's warning.

So the same event receives what looks like praise in Kings and judgement in Hosea. The learner reads this as a change of lens: "What changed? Not God. The people writing about God developed better lenses. Hosea had the courage to say, 'No, that's not what God wanted.'" That is a real reading, held in various forms by Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Eric Seibert and Peter Enns. It is not the only reading. Many commentators argue that Hosea condemns not the commission but how Jehu carried it out: his ambition, his excess (killing Judah's princes and Ahab's friends went beyond the word to strike Ahab's house), and his later idolatry, which 2 Kings 10:31 already notes. Robert Chisholm argues that Hosea uses Jezreel as a pattern: as Jehu's house destroyed Ahab's house there, so Jehu's house will now fall. Others, like Peter Goeman, read "the blood of Jezreel" as the bloodshed's consequences rather than a verdict on Jehu's guilt. Critical scholars often explain the tension by sources: the Kings account comes from circles that celebrated Jehu's anti-Baal revolution; Hosea comes from a prophet who saw Jehu's dynasty as violent and corrupt. And some canonical readers say the Bible deliberately keeps both texts so that later readers learn that God's use of a human instrument is never a blank cheque. The widget below sets these readings side by side.
49908: Accommodation: an old idea with new uses
49909:
"Accommodation" means that God adapts his communication to the capacity of the hearer, as a parent talks to a small child. The idea is ancient. Origen (3rd century) said that Scripture speaks of God's "anger" in the way we speak to children, not because God has human passions. John Chrysostom (late 4th century) spoke often of God's *synkatabasis*, his gracious "condescension" in coming down to our level. John Calvin wrote that God "lisps" to us as nurses do with infants (*Institutes* 1.13.1). Gregory of Nyssa found it unworthy of God that he would kill the innocent firstborn of Egypt for Pharaoh's sin, and read the story spiritually instead (*Life of Moses* 2.91-92).

Notice what these older uses usually meant. For most Fathers and for Calvin, accommodation concerned the *form* of revelation: human words, pictures of God with arms and anger, laws suited to a people's stage. It did not usually mean that God never commanded what the text says he commanded. Augustine, for example, defended the Old Testament wars as just, against the Manichaean Faustus (*Against Faustus* 22).

The modern "cruciform" version goes further. Greg Boyd (*The Crucifixion of the Warrior God*, 2017) argues that God, out of self-giving love, allowed his people to attribute to him violent actions that reflected their fallen, culturally conditioned views. On the cross Jesus bore our sin and appeared as a criminal; in the same way, Boyd says, God "stooped" to bear the ugly image his people projected onto him. Boyd still holds the whole Bible to be inspired: the violent portraits are inspired witnesses to how far God was willing to stoop. Eric Seibert (*Disturbing Divine Behavior*, 2009) distinguishes the "textual God" from the "actual God" revealed in Jesus. Brad Jersak (*A More Christlike God*, 2015) and Peter Enns (*The Bible Tells Me So*, 2014) make related moves. Supporters point to Matthew 19:8, to Ezekiel 20:25 ("I gave them also statutes that were not good"), and to Jeremiah 7:31, where God says child sacrifice "came not into my heart".
49910: The conquest and herem: what are the options?
49911:
The Hebrew word *herem* ("devoted to destruction", often translated "utterly destroy") describes setting something apart for God by removing it completely from human use. In the conquest it is applied to Canaanite cities. Serious Christians read it in at least five ways.

(1) **Just judgement, as written.** God, the giver of life, judged nations whose sin had reached its full measure (Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 18:24-28), using Israel once, in a unique, unrepeatable moment. This is the traditional view of Augustine and many Reformed and evangelical scholars. (2) **Real command, but hyperbolic language.** Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan (*Did God Really Command Genocide?*, 2014) argue that "utterly destroy" is stock war rhetoric in the ancient Near East, like a team that "slaughtered" its rival. The Moabite Stone (around 840 BC) claims that "Israel has utterly perished forever", which was plainly not true. In the Bible, too, Joshua 10:40 says all were destroyed, yet Judges 1 says the Canaanites remained, and Deuteronomy 7:2-3 forbids marrying the same people it says to destroy. On this reading the main goal was driving out and dismantling Canaanite religion, not killing every person. (3) **The "God I don't understand" view.** Christopher Wright admits there is no fully satisfying answer, holds that God did act in judgement, and stresses that the same God promises blessing to all nations and later threatens Israel with the same judgement. David Lamb (*God Behaving Badly*, 2011) shows how much mercy surrounds the hard texts. (4) **Cruciform reinterpretation.** Boyd: Israel heard God's call to possess the land through their violent culture; the cross shows us what God was really like behind that portrait. (5) **Textual God vs actual God.** Seibert and Enns: these are Israel's stories, told the way ancient peoples told war stories, and Christians are not obliged to believe God acted that way.

John and Harvey Walton (*The Lost World of the Israelite Conquest*, 2017) add a further angle: *herem* was about removing a people's identity and order, not about punishing their guilt, which changes the moral question again.
49912: Psalm 137, Elijah's fire and Jesus' rebuke
49913:
Psalm 137 is the cry of exiles who watched Jerusalem burn. It ends: "Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones." Most readers today, of every view, agree that this is an honest prayer of rage handed over to God rather than a command to imitate. The Bible lets traumatised people speak in their own voice. Origen read it allegorically: the "little ones of Babylon" are the first sinful thoughts in the soul, to be dashed against the rock who is Christ (*Against Celsus* 7.22).

In 2 Kings 1 Elijah calls down fire on soldiers sent to arrest him. In Luke 9, when a Samaritan village refuses Jesus, James and John ask, "wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?" Jesus turns and rebukes them. Many later manuscripts add, "Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them" (KJV Luke 9:55-56). These words are missing from the earliest manuscripts, so modern translations put them in a footnote, but the rebuke itself is in all of them. Jesus-lens readers see here a model: Jesus refuses to repeat an Old Testament act that his disciples assumed was a pattern to follow. Other readers answer that Jesus rebukes the disciples' spirit and their misreading of their own mission, not Elijah's prophetic act in its own time.

In the same way, in Luke 4 Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in the synagogue and stops just before "the day of vengeance of our God". Jesus-lens readers find that pause significant; others note that Jesus speaks of judgement elsewhere (Luke 13:1-5; Luke 21:20-24).
49914: Why this matters: violence done in the name of Scripture
49915:
The learner wrote: "Without the Word (Jesus) the Bible becomes deadly. Much violence has taken place in the name of Scripture." History bears this out, and it should be told briefly and accurately.

The First Crusade (preached in 1095) was framed as holy war and pilgrimage; some chroniclers described the slaughter in Jerusalem in 1099 with biblical language. In the Spanish conquest of the Americas, the *Requerimiento* (1513) was read to native peoples demanding submission to the Church and Crown, and in the Valladolid debate (1550–1551) Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda defended the wars partly with Old Testament precedents, while Bartolomé de las Casas answered from the Gospel. Some English Puritan writers in New England described Native Americans with Canaanite and Amalekite imagery. Defenders of slavery in the American South cited the "curse of Ham" (really a curse on Canaan, Genesis 9:25) and the household codes; Thornton Stringfellow's *Scriptural Testimony* (1841) is one example. In South Africa, parts of the Dutch Reformed Church built a theological case for apartheid from Babel and the separation of nations (Genesis 11; Acts 17:26); in 1982 the World Alliance of Reformed Churches declared that defence a heresy, and the Belhar Confession answered it.

These abuses do not by themselves decide which reading of the conquest is right: defenders of the traditional view insist that the conquest was unique and never a licence for later wars, and they point out that Christians who opposed slavery and apartheid also argued from Scripture. But every view must answer this: if a text has been used to kill, how do we read it so that it cannot be used that way again? The Jesus lens says: by Jesus. Traditional readers say: by careful attention to covenant and context, which also leads to Jesus. Both agree the Bible read without Christ and without love has been dangerous.
49917: 2 Kings 10:30 commends Jehu's purge of Ahab's house. Hosea 1:4 announces judgement on Jehu's house for "the blood of Jezreel". Read the two verses side by side, then through each lens.
49918:
2 Kings 10:30: "And the LORD said unto Jehu, Because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes, and hast done unto the house of Ahab according to all that was in mine heart, thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel."

Hosea 1:4: "And the LORD said unto him, Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel." (KJV)
49920: The learner; in related forms Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Eric Seibert, Peter Enns, Brian Zahnd
49921: God did not change; Israel's perception of God did. The writer of Kings understood Jehu's bloodbath as God's will. Hosea, a century later, saw more clearly and said the massacre was not what God wanted. The canon keeps both so that we can watch the lens being corrected, a movement that is completed in Jesus, who refuses violence. Strength: it takes the contradiction at face value. Critique: 2 Kings 9:6-10 has a prophet commission Jehu in God's name, and Hosea himself announces violent judgement on Israel, so Hosea is not a pacifist corrective.
49922: Commission obeyed, but in the wrong spirit
49923: Many traditional commentators (e.g. the Catholic Haydock commentary; many evangelical commentaries)
49924: God did use Jehu to judge Ahab's house, and the act itself is commended. But Jehu went beyond the commission (killing Judah's royal family and Ahab's friends and priests), acted from ambition, and kept the golden calves (2 Kings 10:29-31). Hosea condemns the bloodshed as Jehu actually carried it out. Strength: it explains why 2 Kings 10:31 already qualifies the praise. Critique: Hosea 1:4 does not mention excess or motives; this explanation is brought in from outside.
49925: Jezreel as a pattern of judgement
49926: Robert B. Chisholm Jr. (Bibliotheca Sacra, 2019); Peter Goeman
49927: Hosea is not reversing Kings. "Visit the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu" means that what happened to Ahab's house at Jezreel will now happen to Jehu's house, because it has become just as corrupt. The name Jezreel recalls the place of a dynasty's fall. Strength: it keeps both texts true without a contradiction. Critique: the plain sense of "avenge the blood" (KJV) suggests guilt for bloodshed, and many translations read it that way.
49929: Historical-critical scholarship (common in standard critical commentaries)
49930: 2 Kings 9–10 comes from circles that celebrated Jehu's revolution against the Baal-worshipping Omride dynasty. Hosea, an eighth-century prophet in the north, saw the Jehu dynasty's violence as the root of Israel's ruin. The texts disagree because their authors disagreed. Strength: it is honest about genuine human voices in Scripture. Critique: by itself it says little about how a believing community should hear God through both texts.
49932: Canonical and narrative readers (e.g. in the line of Brevard Childs; many Jewish readers who prize argument within Scripture)
49933: The editors who gathered the Scriptures knew both texts and kept both on purpose. Together they teach that God may use a human instrument without endorsing everything the instrument does, and that a prophet's verdict can expose what a court history celebrated. The tension is a lesson, not a mistake. Strength: it respects the final shape of Scripture. Critique: critics on both sides say it can avoid deciding what God actually wanted.
49934: Approaches to violence in the Old Testament
49935: Each position is held by serious, believing (or in some cases academic) readers. Place your own view, and read the strongest case for the views furthest from you.
49936: God commanded it as written, and it was just
49937: The text reflects human misperception of God, corrected in Christ
49939: Augustine (Against Faustus 22); many Reformed and evangelical scholars, e.g. Clay Jones, Eugene Merrill
49940: God is the Lord of life and judge of all. The Canaanites' sin had reached its full measure (Gen 15:16). The conquest was a unique, limited act of judgement, never a model for later wars. Critique: it is hard to reconcile the killing of infants with Jesus' revelation of God; defenders answer that God takes infants to himself and that our moral sense is itself shaped by God's revelation.
49942: Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan; Nicholas Wolterstorff (on hyperbole)
49943: God did command Israel to dispossess the Canaanites, but "leave nothing alive" is ancient war rhetoric. The main targets were military strongholds and Canaanite religion, and the biblical text itself shows survivors. Critique: 1 Samuel 15 and Joshua 6 seem specific, and hyperbole still leaves God commanding killing.
49944: Real but troubling: the God I don't understand
49945: Christopher J. H. Wright; David T. Lamb; John and Harvey Walton (on herem)
49946: Hold the conquest within the whole story: judgement on sin, God's same judgement later on Israel, and a promise to bless all nations. Admit what we cannot explain. Critique: some find this honest but unresolved; others say it is the only honest place to stand.
49948: Greg Boyd (The Crucifixion of the Warrior God); Brad Jersak; Brian Zahnd
49949: The whole Bible is inspired, but the cross is the lens. Where a portrait of God contradicts the crucified Christ, it shows God stooping to bear his people's fallen views, as he bore our sin on the cross. Critique: who decides which portraits are fallen? Jesus himself affirms Old Testament judgement stories (Matt 24:37-39) and the New Testament contains judgement too.
49952: These are Israel's own stories, told the way ancient peoples told war stories. We may honour them as Scripture without believing God actually did these things. Jesus is the standard. Critique: it can make the reader the judge of Scripture and risks the old error of Marcion, who split the God of Israel from the Father of Jesus.
49954: Many secular and critical scholars (e.g. Hector Avalos)
49955: The texts are human products reflecting ancient nationalism and should be judged by modern ethics. No divine meaning is sought. Critique (from believers of every view): it does not read the Bible as Scripture at all, and it cannot explain why the same texts produced the prophets' and Jesus' ethic of love for enemies.
49956: How the church has handled violent texts
49957: A short, selective history. Some dates are approximate.
49959: Marcion taught that the violent God of the Old Testament was a lesser god than the Father of Jesus. The church at Rome rejected him and kept the Old Testament as Christian Scripture.
49961: Origen answers a pagan critic: God's "wrath" is accommodated language, and Psalm 137 and other violent texts are to be read spiritually (Against Celsus 4.71-72; 7.22).
49962: In The Life of Moses Gregory finds the killing of Egypt's innocent firstborn unworthy of God if read only literally, and reads it as the destruction of evil at its beginning.
49964: Augustine defends the Old Testament wars as just acts commanded by God against the Manichaean critic Faustus; this becomes the main Western view.
49966: Pope Urban II preaches the Crusade at Clermont. Holy-war language, partly drawn from the Old Testament, is applied to a new war.
49968: Sepúlveda defends the Spanish wars in the Americas partly with Old Testament precedents; Las Casas argues from the Gospel for peaceful conversion.
49969: Calvin's teaching on accommodation (God "lisps" to us, Institutes 1.13.1) shapes Protestant reading, though he still holds the commands to be God's.
49971: Thornton Stringfellow and others defend American slavery from Genesis 9 and the household codes; abolitionists answer from Scripture too.
49973: The World Alliance of Reformed Churches declares the biblical defence of apartheid a heresy; the Belhar Confession is drafted the same year.
49975: Distinguishes the "textual God" from the "actual God" revealed in Jesus.
49976: Copan, Is God a Moral Monster?
49977: A popular defence of the Old Testament ethic, later developed with Flannagan in Did God Really Command Genocide? (2014).
49978: A two-volume case for a cruciform hermeneutic: the cross as the lens for every portrait of God.
49979: quoted in the learner's course notes
49980: As nurses commonly do with infants, God is wont in a measure to 'lisp' in speaking to us.
49981: Institutes of the Christian Religion 1.13.1 (Beveridge translation)
49982: Developing perception, corrected in Christ (the Jesus lens)
49983: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Eric Seibert, Peter Enns, Bill Johnson's "Jesus is perfect theology"; the learner
49984: God has always been like Jesus. The Old Testament is an inspired, honest record of a people's real but developing and often flawed perception of that God. God accommodated himself to their violent, tribal world (Matt 19:8) to lead them on, and allowed his reputation to be marred by their portraits. Jesus, the exact imprint of God's nature (Heb 1:3) and his "exegesis" (John 1:18), shows who God has been all along. Jesus modelled this himself: "You have heard that it was said... but I say to you" (Matt 5:38-44).
49985: It takes the moral problem seriously instead of explaining it away. It makes Jesus, not a single verse, the final word about God. It has precedent in the Fathers' unease with literal readings, and the canon itself shows development (Hosea on Jezreel, Ezek 20:25, Jer 7:31). It guards against using Scripture to justify violence.
49986: Jesus affirmed the Old Testament strongly (Matt 5:17-18; John 10:35) and treated its judgement stories as real (Luke 17:26-32). The New Testament also contains divine judgement (Acts 5:1-11; 2 Thess 1:6-9; Rev 19:11-16). Who decides what is "Christlike"? There is a risk of shaping Jesus in our own image and drifting toward Marcion. Boyd answers that he keeps every text as inspired; critics reply that calling a text an inspired record of error is still a major change.
49987: Just judgement in a unique moment
49988: Augustine; much of the Reformed and evangelical tradition (e.g. Eugene Merrill in Show Them No Mercy, 2003; Clay Jones)
49989: God, who gives life, has the right to take it. The conquest was judgement on long-tolerated evil (Gen 15:16; Lev 18:24-28), limited to one land and one time, and the same God later judged Israel by the same standard. It is not a model for anyone today. The cross does not cancel God's justice; it shows that he bore it himself.
49990: It accepts the text as it stands and fits Jesus' high view of Scripture. It holds that love and judgement belong together in both Testaments. It keeps God's moral authority above ours.
49991: It struggles with the killing of children and with how such texts have been used. Jesus-lens readers say it lets the Old Testament picture define God and then fits Jesus into it, rather than the reverse.
49993: Paul Copan (Is God a Moral Monster?, 2011); Copan and Matthew Flannagan (Did God Really Command Genocide?, 2014)
